title: Area VIII review: Instrument Approach Procedures
intro: These questions mix the five Tasks of Area VIII the way the checkride does: the evaluator selects Tasks A and B and combines them with a missed approach, a circling approach or a straight-in landing, and at least one nonprecision approach is flown without the attitude and heading indicators (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area VIII NOTE). Expect a glideslope that fails into a localizer approach, an LPV that loses its vertical guidance, a partial-panel approach that ends in a circle, an ILS that ends in a published or ATC missed approach, a climb gradient the airplane cannot meet, circling categories, radii and restrictions, and straight-in landings in gusts, wake turbulence and wind shear.

questions.q: ATIS at Troy says the glideslope is out of service. Cairns Approach clears your Category A learner for the "ILS or LOC runway 7 approach" and says nothing about it. The local altimeter setting is available, and he will fly 90 knots. He briefs DA 600, sure that ATC would have warned him if the glideslope were out. What do you teach?
options: Fly the S-ILS line to DA 600: ATC said nothing about the glideslope, so the clearance is still for the ILS
Fly the S-LOC line: MDA 880 as a floor, below it only with references, missed at I-TOI 0.9 DME or 3:04 from BLOOD
Fly the S-LOC line, but treat 880 as a DA and start the missed approach the moment he gets there without the runway
Fly the S-LOC line with DA 701 and 1 mile, since the chart raises the minimums whenever a component is out
questions.why: With the glideslope out, the ILS becomes a nonprecision localizer approach [[33:83|AIM 1-1-9j]]. ATC uses the published name and must say that a failed component is unusable, except when the title already allows for it, as "ILS or LOC" does [[33:424|AIM 5-4-7h]], so the silence proves nothing. On the chart the S-LOC 7 line is 880-1 for A and B, the MAP is at I-TOI 0.9 DME, and the FAF-to-MAP table gives 3:04 at 90 knots; DA 701 comes from the Montgomery altimeter note, not from a failed glideslope [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]]. An MDA is the lowest altitude to which descent is authorized on final [[29:159|IPH 4-19]], and a nonprecision MAP is a fix or a time from the FAF [[29:181|IPH 4-41]], so treating 880 as a DA throws away the level segment to the MAP. At the MAP without the 91.175(c) requirements the missed approach is required [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]]: climb to 1300, then a climbing right turn to 2200 direct BLOOD and hold [[23:310|IFH Figure 10-11]].

questions.q: On the Monroeville RNAV (GPS) RWY 3, your Category A learner levels at the 840 LNAV MDA (HAT 422). No VDP is charted. Rain hides the field until he sees the REIL about 0.5 NM from the threshold at 90 knots groundspeed, with the published visibility. He says REIL is a listed reference, so he may land. What do you teach?
options: Continue straight in: REIL is on the 91.175(c) list and the visibility is there, so the rule is fully met
Continue straight in, cutting the power and adding flaps, since below the MDA no descent rate limit applies
Stay at 840 until the MAP over the threshold, then descend, since with no VDP the MAP is the descent point
Not straight in: from 422 ft at half a mile he needs about 1,270 fpm, so he is not in position for a normal descent
questions.why: Going below the MDA needs all three parts of 91.175(c), and the first is being continuously in a position to descend to the runway at a normal rate using normal maneuvers [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]]; REIL and visibility alone are the tempting half answer. At 90 knots, 0.5 NM takes 20 seconds, so losing 422 ft needs about 1,270 fpm, and a descent rate over about 1,000 fpm below 1,000 ft AGL is unacceptable in either the instrument or the visual part of an approach [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]. The AIM warns that close in, between a VDP and the MAP, a descent below the MDA may be inadvisable or impossible, judged by speed, height above the runway, descent rate and runway length [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h]]. With no VDP charted, the IPH says to calculate a descent point: at 300 ft per NM, a 422 ft HAT means leaving the MDA about 1.4 NM out [[29:177|IPH 4-37]] [[29:179|IPH 4-39]]. Reaching the MDA at a MAP on the threshold may force a missed approach [[29:177|IPH 4-37]], and at the MAP without the requirements he must go missed [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]].

questions.q: Your learner flies the Oklahoma City RNAV (GPS) RWY 35L to the LPV line. Inside IMZUY, descending through 2,200 ft, the vertical guidance flags off while the lateral guidance stays good. What do you teach?
options: Keep descending to the 1530 LPV DA, holding the 3° rate from the table, since the lateral guidance is still LPV
Go missed at once, since a WAAS receiver cannot be flown to any other line of minima after the approach is active
If his operating rules allow the change, fly the LNAV line: 1580 as an MDA, the VDP, and the missed at RW35L
Change to the LNAV/VNAV line and treat 1580 as a DA, so a short dip below it during the missed is allowed
questions.why: Receivers do not fail down once the approach is active, but if only the vertical flag appears, the pilot may elect the LNAV minima if the rules under which the flight is operating allow changing the approach after starting it [[33:105|AIM 1-1-18d2]]. So an automatic missed approach is not required, and a descent to the LPV DA without vertical guidance is not an LPV approach at all. LNAV/VNAV also needs vertical guidance, from baro-VNAV or WAAS [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(c)]]. On the chart the LNAV MDA is 1580, with a VDP 0.8 NM from RW35L for LNAV only [[29:164|IPH Figure 4-12]]. Only a DA allows a momentary descent below it during the change to the missed; below an MDA the 91.175 conditions must be met [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m5(a)]] [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m6(b)]], and VDPs apply to LP and LNAV minima [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m7(b)]].

questions.q: For the required no-gyro nonprecision approach you simulate a vacuum failure, as in the figure. Your learner reaches the circling MDA and starts a circle to land. On downwind, rain hides the whole airport. He says he will hold the MDA and keep turning until he sees it again. What do you teach?
options: Hold the MDA and keep circling, since he is still inside the area where the MDA gives 300 ft of clearance
Turn straight to the published missed approach course, timing a standard-rate turn on the turn coordinator
Go missed now: a climbing turn toward the landing runway on the turn coordinator, with small, precise inputs
Descend under the rain to find the airport, since inside the circling area the clearance also extends below the MDA
questions.why: During a circle at or above the MDA, a missed approach is required at once when no identifiable part of the airport is distinctly visible, unless only a normal bank hides it [[60:473|14 CFR 91.175(e)(2)]]. The AIM has the pilot make an initial climbing turn toward the landing runway and keep turning until established on the missed approach course, which keeps him inside the protected areas; turning straight to the missed approach course is the tempting wrong answer [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21c]] [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21c]]. The 300 ft of obstacle clearance is for an airplane at or above the circling altitude [[29:149|IPH 4-9]], and below the MDA the pilot must see and avoid obstacles [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]]. On partial panel the turn coordinator is primary for bank [[23:182|IFH 7-21]], and only small, precise inputs work, since rapid ones compound a deviation [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].

questions.q: A NOTAM puts the Hilltop VOR out of service. Your learner's destination has a VOR RWY 27 whose final approach course comes from that VOR, with no "or GPS" in the title, and an ILS RWY 9 whose missed approach goes to the VOR and holds there. His airplane has an IFR-approved GPS with a current database. Which approach can he plan?
options: The ILS, using the GPS to fly the missed approach to the VOR's position and hold there, but not the VOR approach
Both: a suitable GPS can stand in for the VOR anywhere on either approach, the final approach course included
Neither: once a NOTAM takes the VOR out, every procedure that uses it is unusable, even with an approved GPS
The VOR approach as well, if he hears the VOR's identifier on the way in, since that shows it is back on the air
questions.why: A suitable RNAV system, such as an IFR-approved GPS, may substitute for an out-of-service VOR, including navigating to it and holding over it [[33:116|AIM 1-2-3]] [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3]], so the ILS missed approach can still be flown; the database should be current, and he may need to tell ATC of the plan [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3]]. But a pilot may not substitute for the NAVAID that gives lateral guidance on the final approach segment, unless the title has "or GPS" [[33:118|AIM 1-2-3]], which rules out the VOR approach and the tempting "both" answer. Hearing an identifier proves nothing: do not fly a procedure NOTAMed out of service even if the identification is present [[33:87|AIM 1-1-11]].

questions.q: Your learner flies the Orlando Executive ILS RWY 7 to the 309 DA. Nothing is in sight, so he goes around and plans to climb straight ahead to 1,500, then turn left toward OVIDO once he is settled. What do you correct?
options: Nothing: the 1200 limit on this chart applies only to a missed approach that is started before the MAP
Turn left toward OVIDO right at the DA, since on an ILS the missed approach point and the turn are both there
Climb on the localizer east course, no higher than 1,200, until SOTCO, then a climbing left turn to 1,500
Climb to 1,200, then turn left at once onto ORL R-049, since the turn on this missed is not tied to any fix
questions.why: On a precision approach the MAP is where the airplane reaches the DA on the glideslope [[29:181|IPH 4-41]], and at the DA without the required references the missed approach is immediate [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]]. The published text is the whole procedure: climb to 1200 maximum altitude via the I-ORL east course to SOTCO (ORL 1.5 DME or radar), then a climbing left turn to 1500 via ORL R-049 to OVIDO and hold [[29:184|IPH Figure 4-23]]. The note about descending to 1200 on an early missed is a separate limit before the MAP [[29:181|IPH 4-41]]; it does not remove the 1200 maximum in the missed approach text. After a DA the airplane follows the missed instructions along the final course to at least the threshold or MAP before any turns [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m5(a)]], so an immediate turn is wrong. Then report the missed approach and ask for what comes next [[34:4|AIM 5-5-5a2]] [[34:5|AIM 5-5-5a6]].

questions.q: The weather is 400 overcast and 1 mile. Without any request from your learner, approach turns him onto the localizer with a 45° intercept about 1 NM outside the FAF. He overshoots, chases the needle and is still correcting at the FAF. What do you teach him?
options: Accept it as normal: in any weather ATC may turn him onto the localizer that close, so he must cope with it
In this weather the intercept should be at least 3 NM outside the FAF; ask for room, and turn at first needle movement
Next time ask to be turned on inside the FAF, since ATC may give a pilot any intercept he asks for, even inside it
Hold the 45° heading until the needle centers, then turn inbound, since an early turn wastes the intercept angle
questions.why: Controllers must ensure the intercept is at least 2 NM outside the approach gate, a point 1 NM outside the FAF, so about 3 NM out [[29:193|IPH 4-53]] [[29:194|IPH 4-54]]. Closer intercepts are allowed only with a ceiling at least 500 ft above the MVA/MIA and at least 3 SM visibility (no closer than the gate), or at the pilot's request (no closer than the FAF) [[29:194|IPH 4-54]], so 400 and 1 does not qualify, and no one turns him on inside the FAF. A pilot who feels rushed on vectors can ask for a delay or a vector that gives more time [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. A large intercept angle usually overshoots; turn to the localizer heading at the first needle movement [[23:285|IFH 9-42]], and the final vector should let him get established before the FAF [[33:396|AIM 5-4-3b1(c)]].

questions.q: At night Gulfport Tower is closed and no local altimeter setting is available, so your Category A learner will use Pascagoula's. His airplane has an IFR GPS with approach-approved baro-VNAV but no WAAS. Which line and minimums do you brief for the RNAV (GPS) RWY 14?
options: LNAV/VNAV: DA 531, which is 464 plus 67, with the visibility raised to RVR 6000 by the chart note
LPV: DA 294, which is 227 plus 67, since the higher DA keeps the vertical guidance legal with Pascagoula
LNAV: MDA 440 and the VDP, since the Pascagoula note raises only the lines that are flown to a DA
LNAV: MDA 520, which is 440 plus 80, and no VDP, since baro-VNAV is NA with the Pascagoula setting
questions.why: The chart notes say that without the local setting, use Pascagoula's and increase all DAs 67 ft and all MDAs 80 ft, and that VDP and baro-VNAV are NA when using the Pascagoula setting [[23:307|IFH Figure 10-9]]. The AIM agrees: baro-VNAV must be flown using the local altimeter setting only, and when the local setting is not available the LNAV/VNAV line can still be used by WAAS receivers [[33:399|AIM 5-4-5a4]], so the tempting LNAV/VNAV answer needs equipment he lacks. LPV needs WAAS equipment with an AFM statement that it supports LPV [[33:416|AIM 5-4-5m1(b)]]. That leaves LNAV at 440 + 80 = 520, flown as an MDA [[33:418|AIM 5-4-5m6(b)]], and the note applies to all MDAs, not only the DAs.

questions.q: On the ILS at about 700 ft AGL, your learner's glideslope needle shows one dot fly-up, like the lower airplane in the figure, and the airspeed is 10 knots above his target. He adds power to climb back to the glideslope. What do you teach?
options: Add power and raise the nose, since any time he is low on the glideslope the airplane needs more total energy
Low and fast is energy in the wrong place: raise the nose to trade speed for height, without adding power
Reduce power first to get rid of the extra speed, then fix the glideslope once he is back on his target speed
Hold the attitude and let the needle come back on its own, since he need not correct before full-scale deflection
questions.why: The AFH sorts path and speed errors by energy: lower-and-slower is a lack of total energy, fixed with the throttle, while lower-and-faster is a distribution error, fixed by pulling back on the yoke to trade speed for height [[24:98|AFH 4-12]]. Adding power to a low-and-fast airplane leaves it fast once it is back on the path. Cutting power first sinks it further below the glideslope, and the AIM says to avoid flying below the glide path to keep obstacle and terrain clearance [[33:81|AIM 1-1-9d5]]. The glideslope is so sensitive that very small corrections keep the airplane on it [[23:283|IFH 9-40]], and a stabilized approach needs the airspeed back within +10/-5 knots of the target [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

questions.q: A runway closure leaves only a 3° ILS with a 15-knot tailwind. Your learner flies his approaches at 105 knots and always sets 500 fpm on the glideslope. What do you brief before the approach?
options: Plan about 637 fpm for 120 knots over the ground, and a longer landing roll to check against the runway
Keep 500 fpm, since the glideslope angle stays 3° whatever the wind does along the final approach course
Plan about 557 fpm, reading the table at 105 knots, since the airspeed, not the wind, sets the descent rate
Plan about 637 fpm, and a shorter landing roll, since he touches down at his usual indicated airspeed
questions.why: Pilots use the angle and the actual or estimated groundspeed to find the rate of descent [[23:42|IFH 1-23]]: 105 knots plus a 15-knot tailwind is 120 knots, and the table gives 637 fpm for 3.0° at 120 knots [[23:44|IFH Figure 1-19]]. The quick rule, groundspeed times 5, gives 600 fpm [[29:116|IPH 3-4]]. A fixed 500 fpm would leave him sinking below the glideslope, which the AIM says to avoid [[33:81|AIM 1-1-9d5]]; with the proper rate set at interception only very small corrections are needed [[23:283|IFH 9-40]]. A tailwind also means a longer landing roll, because the airplane touches down at a higher groundspeed [[28:132|AWH 10-17]], so the landing distance must be checked against the runway length [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]].

questions.q: Your learner plans the Daggett RNAV (GPS) RWY 26 on a hot afternoon. His POH shows a climb of about 420 fpm, and with the true airspeed and a tailwind he expects 120 knots groundspeed on the missed. He wants the lower LPV DA # line, 2217-1. What do you teach?
options: Fly the 2217 line, since the # gradient is only a planning figure; if he falls short, he tells ATC his climb rate
Fly the 2217 line, since the 220 ft/NM climb is needed only after he reaches the NULMN holding fix
Brief the 2438-1¾ line: 220 ft/NM at 120 knots needs about 440 fpm, more than his airplane can climb
Fly the 2217 line, since the # gradient applies only to Category C and D airplanes on this missed
questions.why: The note says the missed approach requires a minimum climb of 220 ft per NM to 8000, and the two LPV lines show the choice: the lower DA # needs that gradient, the higher 2438 line does not [[29:187|IPH Figure 4-26]] [[29:181|IPH 4-41]]. Pilots must preplan that the airplane can meet the gradient, and a higher groundspeed raises the climb rate needed [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]]. In the TPP table the rate in fpm equals the gradient at 60 knots and doubles at 120 knots (297 ft/NM: 297 and 595 fpm) [[29:34|IPH Figure 1-17]], so 220 ft/NM at 120 knots needs about 440 fpm, more than his 420. The higher line needs only the standard 200 ft/NM [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]], about 400 fpm at 120 knots, which he can make. The gradient runs to 8000, not from the hold, and the note names no categories. A pilot unable to climb at least 500 fpm should report it to ATC [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1(c)]], but a report does not replace the preplanning the AIM requires.

questions.q: On an LNAV approach with a non-WAAS GPS, 2 NM past the FAWP and descending toward the MDA, your learner gets a RAIM annunciation. He levels off and plans to continue to the MAWP to look for the runway. What do you teach?
options: Climb and fly the missed approach now, treat the GPS as advisory, and report the GPS anomaly to ATC
Continue to the MAWP at the MDA, since a RAIM alert after the FAWP still leaves the approach usable
Continue the descent to the MDA, since the receiver keeps navigating and the alert is for information only
Climb to the missed approach altitude, but wait until RAIM returns before saying anything to ATC about it
questions.why: If the RAIM annunciation appears after the FAWP, the pilot should start a climb and fly the missed approach; the receiver may keep working, but its information is advisory only [[33:98|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)(8)]]. The rule before the FAWP is different: do not descend, and go to the MAWP via the FAWP for the missed [[33:98|AIM 1-1-17b5(g)(7)]], which is the version the learner half-remembers. A missed approach and a GPS anomaly with an installed IFR GPS are both reports made without an ATC request [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1(d)]] [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3a1(h)]], and 91.187 requires reporting a navigation or approach malfunction as soon as practical [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187(a)]], so waiting is wrong. Unless ATC clears otherwise, an early missed still follows the procedure to the MAP before turning [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]].

questions.q: At a nontowered field your learner breaks out on an RNAV approach and leaves the MDA in position to land. At about 200 ft above the runway a deer runs onto it. He says he will call Center for a new clearance first and then decide. What do you teach?
options: Land long, beyond the deer, since below the MDA the published missed approach gives him no protection
Call Center first for an amended clearance, then add power once he knows where ATC wants him to go
Go around now: power, attitude, flaps up in steps; fly the balked-landing plan he briefed, then call ATC
Climb straight to the published missed approach altitude, since from there the published missed protects him
questions.why: A missed approach is required for a rejected landing for any reason, such as animals on the runway [[29:180|IPH 4-40]]. At an airport without an operating control tower the pilot should fly the go-around or missed approach without delay and contact ATC when able [[33:453|AIM 5-4-21h]], so calling first has it backwards. Power, attitude, configuration is the order, with the flaps up in small steps [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. A missed started below the MDA is not necessarily protected by the published procedure [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21h]], which is why the pilot should assess the actions for a balked landing below the MDA before starting the approach [[33:453|AIM 5-4-21h]]. That is a reason to brief the go-around, not to land toward an animal on the runway.

questions.q: With the attitude and heading indicators covered, your learner reaches the MAP with nothing in sight. He jams in full power and hauls the nose up "to feel the climb," and the airspeed drops 15 knots below his climb speed. What do you teach?
options: Keep pulling until the VSI shows a strong climb, since on partial panel the VSI is the primary pitch instrument
Smooth full power and a small pitch change; hold climb speed on the airspeed indicator, and trim
Fly the pitch his body feels is right, since without an attitude indicator the inner ear is the best cue
Stay level at the MDA past the MAP until the gyros recover, then start the climb with full power
questions.why: Full power goes in smoothly and without hesitation, since abrupt throttle movement can make some engines falter, and the pilot should resist pitching up when the airspeed is not there, because the airplane cannot climb below minimum power required speed [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. In a stabilized climb the airspeed indicator is primary for pitch, and partial panel climb entries go best from climbing speed [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. With limited instruments only small, precise inputs work; rapid ones cause oscillation [[23:197|IFH 7-36]]. A rapid acceleration can create the somatogravic illusion of a nose-up attitude, so the body is a poor guide [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. Staying level past the MAP breaks the rule to go missed there [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]].

questions.q: Four miles out on the ILS, the tower says: "Go around, traffic on the runway. Fly runway heading, climb and maintain 3,000." Your learner starts the published missed approach, a climbing right turn at 1,300, because the approach clearance included it. What do you teach?
options: Fly the published missed, since the approach clearance already included it and a later instruction cannot replace it
Fly the published missed, but hold the right turn until the MAP, since an early missed never turns before the MAP
Continue to the DA and go around there, since ATC cannot cancel an approach once the airplane is established
Fly runway heading and climb to 3,000 as told, since ATC's instructions now take the place of the published missed
questions.why: A pilot flies a missed approach when instructed by ATC [[34:4|AIM 5-5-5a1(c)]], and complies with the published missed approach unless other missed approach instructions are specified by ATC [[34:4|AIM 5-5-5a3]]. The approach clearance includes the published missed only unless ATC instructs otherwise [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21h]], and controllers may vector a radar-identified airplane on a missed approach [[34:5|AIM 5-5-5b2]]. Except in an emergency, no one may operate contrary to an ATC instruction [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(b)]], which rules out continuing to the DA. The fly-to-the-MAP rule for an early missed applies unless ATC clears otherwise [[33:450|AIM 5-4-21b]], so it does not override a heading from the tower.

questions.q: Your Category A learner's flaps fail during a VOR approach, and his POH no-flap speed puts the circle at 125 knots. The circling line on the chart has no C symbol. Which minimums and protected radius apply?
options: Category A minimums and 1.3 NM, since the airplane is certified in Category A and that never changes
Category B minimums and 1.5 NM, since 125 knots is only a little above the Category A speed range
Category C minimums and 2.8 NM, the expanded Category C radius at a 1,001-3,000 ft MDA
Category C minimums and 1.7 NM, the standard radius used when the circling line has no C symbol
questions.why: Category C runs from 121 to less than 141 knots [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]]. An airplane flown faster than its category's range must use the higher category's minimums, inoperative flaps are one of the IPH examples, and the certified category only means it may never use a slower one [[29:148|IPH 4-8]]. Circling minimums protect only within the area for the category speed [[29:148|IPH 4-8]]. With no C symbol the area is the standard one, with fixed radii by category [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]]: 1.7 NM for Category C, while 2.8 NM is an expanded-area figure for charts that carry the C [[33:448|AIM FIG 5-4-28]].

questions.q: Circling at 90 KIAS in his Category A airplane with a strong wind, your learner sees 115 knots groundspeed on downwind. He says that makes him Category B, so he may use the Category B radius and fly a wider pattern. What do you teach?
options: He stays in Category A, since category speeds are indicated airspeeds; he must start his turns early to stay inside
He is right: the category comes from his speed over the ground, so the Category B line and radius now apply
He stays in Category A, but he may drift outside the radius on downwind, since the area design allows for wind
He should slow to 75 KIAS on downwind, so his groundspeed falls below 91 knots and keeps him in Category A
questions.why: Category speeds are indicated airspeeds [[29:148|IPH 4-8]], so 90 KIAS is still Category A [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]]. The AIM warns that on a downwind leg the groundspeed can be much higher than the indicated airspeed, so the pilot must plan the start of every turn to stay inside the circling area [[33:423|AIM 5-4-7c3]]; nothing gives extra room for wind, and the pilot remains within the radius for the category [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f4]]. Slowing down to change a groundspeed number misreads the rule. A late turn with a tailwind leads to an overshoot of final, where the safe answer is a go-around, not a steeper or skidding turn [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

questions.q: By day at Charlotte, your learner flies the ILS or LOC RWY 18L at 110 knots in his Category B airplane, which has no DME; the approach radar is working. The tower tells him to circle to land on Runway 23. He plans to follow the glideslope to the 998 DA and start the circle there. What do you teach?
options: Follow the glideslope to DA 998 and circle from there, staying inside 1.8 NM of the runways
Descend no lower than the 1320 circling MDA, circle inside 1.8 NM, and use the localizer MAP, not the DA
Descend no lower than 1320 and circle inside 1.5 NM, the Category B radius on every circling line
Descend no lower than 1500 with 2¼ miles, since a circle from an ILS always takes the Category C line
questions.why: Circling minimums apply when it is necessary to circle, and the pilot flies no lower than them until in position for a final descent to land [[23:311|IFH 10-20]]. At 110 knots the airplane is Category B [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]], and the chart's circling line for A and B is 1320-1 (HAA 572); the ZIMOG fix line needs DME [[29:214|IPH Figure 4-45]]. The C symbol on the line means the expanded area, sized by category and MDA [[33:447|AIM 5-4-20b1]]: 1.8 NM for Category B at an MDA of 1,001 to 3,000 ft, while 1.5 NM is the old standard radius [[33:448|AIM FIG 5-4-28]]. Circling and nonprecision procedures share the same MAP, found by timing or a fix, and the DA is the MAP only for vertically guided approaches; circling from an ILS needs a localizer line of minima [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f5]].

questions.q: At a nontowered Class G airport, your learner flies an RNAV (GPS) approach to Runway 3 and must circle to land on Runway 21. A chart note says "Circling NA E of Rwy 3-21," and the airport shows no right-traffic markings. He plans a left downwind for 21 because 91.126 requires left turns. What do you teach?
options: Fly the left downwind east of the runway, since the 91.126 turn rule outranks a chart note on circling
Circle west of the runway with right turns, and at the FAF announce the runway and the circling direction
Circle west with right turns, but skip the CTAF calls, since ATC separates an IFR flight down to the runway
Circling is not allowed at all under this note, so he must land straight in on Runway 3 with the tailwind
questions.why: At non-towered airports the pilot uses the 91.126(b) turn direction unless a published circling restriction requires turns in the opposite direction [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f3]], and no circling may be done in the restricted area [[33:450|AIM 5-4-20f1]]. A left downwind for Runway 21 lies east of the runway, so the circle must use right turns on the west side; the left turns of 91.126(b) are the default, not an override [[60:451|14 CFR 91.126(b)]]. The note closes only the east side, not the whole circle. Because ATC cannot separate IFR and VFR traffic where there is no radar coverage, the IPH lists self-announced CTAF calls, including FAF inbound with the landing runway and the maneuvering direction if circling [[29:156|IPH 4-16]].

questions.q: Your learner's autopilot will hold the circling MDA of 1,040 ft, and its altitude preselector moves only in 100-ft steps. How do you teach him to use the preselector from the final approach through the circle?
options: Set 1,100 for the descent; once level in altitude hold, set the missed approach altitude
Set 1,000, the nearest step, and leave it there through the circle so the autopilot holds it on a missed
Set 1,100 and leave it there through the circle, since a new altitude would start a climb in altitude hold
Set the field elevation, so the autopilot can fly the descent once he is in position to land
questions.why: The IPH has the MDA set so the airplane cannot inadvertently descend below it, rounded up when the selector moves in 100-ft steps: 700 ft for a 660 ft MDA [[29:176|IPH 4-36]], so 1,000 is below the MDA. The pitch mode stays in altitude hold until another mode is selected, and once level the missed approach altitude is set, because accurate flight director guidance is not available for a missed approach if the MDA is left in the window [[29:176|IPH 4-36]] [[29:177|IPH 4-37]]. The MDA is still the floor until the airplane is in position to descend for a normal landing [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20f]]. The AFM gives the procedures and limits for using a particular autopilot on an approach [[29:176|IPH 4-36]].

questions.q: Your Category A learner flies an LPV to Runway 14 with the wind 180 at 14 gusting 26, a 12-knot gust factor. His normal approach speed is 80 knots. He plans 80 knots, full flaps and idle power as he crosses the threshold. What do you teach for the final and the landing?
options: About 86 knots with partial flaps; crab, then wing-low before the round out; power on until the mains touch
80 knots with full flaps for the slowest touchdown, and close the throttle at the DA so the gusts can't float him
About 106 knots, his speed plus the whole 26-knot gust, and so he must brief the Category B line for the LPV
About 86 knots with full flaps; hold the crab all the way through touchdown, and idle power at the threshold
questions.why: In turbulence the AFH uses a power-on approach slightly above normal speed, partial flaps in a gusty crosswind, and often the normal speed plus one-half the gust factor, within the AFM/POH; the throttle goes to idle only after the main wheels touch, because closing it early can cause a sudden sink and a hard landing [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. Half of 12 is 6, so about 86 knots, still Category A [[60:724|14 CFR 97.3]]. A gust raises lift and may balloon the airplane, and the lull that follows makes it sink [[28:132|AWH 10-17]]. The crab must come out just before touchdown to avoid a side load; on a long final the pilot may crab first and change to wing-low before the round out [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

questions.q: On the ILS, the tower tells your learner that a Boeing 757 is landing ahead on the same runway. He plans to fly a dot below the glideslope and touch down in the first few hundred feet, short of the 757's touchdown point, "to stay under its wake." What do you teach?
options: Good plan: vortices sink and then rise off the runway, so short of the jet's touchdown point is the safest place
Stay on the glideslope but land short of the jet's touchdown point, since its wake begins only where it lands
Fly the dot low only if the tower warns of wake turbulence, since otherwise ATC is keeping him clear of it
Stay at or above the 757's path, so on or above the glideslope; note its touchdown point and land beyond it
questions.why: Landing behind a larger aircraft on the same runway: stay at or above its final approach flight path, note its touchdown point, and land beyond it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. An aircraft generates vortices from rotation to touchdown, and they sink several hundred feet per minute, so pilots fly at or above the preceding aircraft's path [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]]; the area short of the jet's touchdown point is exactly where its wake lies. Whether or not a warning is given, the pilot is expected to adjust the flight path to preclude serious wake encounters [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. The AIM also says to avoid flying below the glide path to keep obstacle and terrain clearance [[33:81|AIM 1-1-9d5]].

questions.q: Inbound on the ILS, 6 miles out, your learner hears the tower: "Runway 17 arrival microburst alert, 40 knot loss 3 mile final." A rain shaft hangs over the final. He says it will have weakened by the time he gets there, and he will carry 10 extra knots. What do you teach?
options: Continue with the extra speed, since a microburst loses most of its strength within a minute of reaching the ground
Continue to the DA and decide there, since the alert matters only if the runway is still not in sight at minimums
Break off the approach now, tell ATC why and ask to hold or divert, since it may still be getting stronger
Continue, holding the glideslope with pitch alone, since the headwind and tailwind cancel out across a microburst
questions.why: The alert is a microburst with a 40-knot loss on his final [[33:250|AIM 4-3-7]]. A microburst intensifies for about 5 minutes after it strikes the ground, its downdrafts can reach 6,000 fpm, and the shear across it can reach 90 knots [[34:108|AIM 7-1-24]]. Some microbursts cannot be escaped with any known technique [[28:266|AWH 22-11]]. A headwind shear followed by a tailwind or downdraft is particularly dangerous, recovery at low altitude may be impossible, and the IFH says to be ready to go missed at the first indication [[23:316|IFH 10-25]]; in the AWH example the airplane met an increasing downdraft and tailwind and hit short of the runway [[28:271|AWH 22-16]]. A pilot who decides a safe approach or landing is not possible flies a missed approach, tells ATC the reason, and asks for specific action such as holding or an alternate [[34:4|AIM 5-5-5a1(b)]] [[34:4|AIM 5-5-5a2]] [[34:5|AIM 5-5-5a6]].

questions.q: A thunderstorm is moving toward the airport as your learner flies a LOC approach to an MDA. His altimeter setting is 20 minutes old, and the gusts are building. He plans to land before the storm arrives. What do you teach?
options: Fly it as set: an old setting is off by a few feet at most, and the MDA has a margin built in for that
Add 100 ft to the MDA on his own and continue to land, since that covers both the error and the gust front
Land with full flaps at his slowest speed, since a slow touchdown is safest when a gust front is coming
Get a current setting, since pressure swings can cause over 100 ft of error, and don't land ahead of the storm
questions.why: Pressure usually falls rapidly as a thunderstorm approaches and rises sharply with the first gust, a cycle that may take 15 minutes, and without a corrected setting the altimeter may be more than 100 ft in error [[28:274|AWH 22-19]], so 100 ft added on his own may not cover it. The AWH says not to land or take off in the face of an approaching thunderstorm, because a sudden gust front can cause loss of control [[28:276|AWH 22-21]], and the IFH says the dangerous headwind-then-tailwind shear is likely on an approach in the face of an oncoming thunderstorm [[23:316|IFH 10-25]]. In gusts the AFH uses a power-on approach slightly above normal speed with partial flaps, not the slowest possible touchdown [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].
